newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: U.S. said aiming to get financial services pact.
newsitem.headline: U.S. said aiming to get financial services pact.

text.p: Envoys from major powers and emerging economies began a round of bilateral talks on Monday aimed at shaping a global pact by the end of the year to open up markets for financial services.

Before the discussions got under way, a U.S. official said that Washington, which stood aloof from an interim deal involving 43 countries just two years ago, was "committed to try to make this negotiation a success".

Participation by the United States, the world's largest single market in the sector, is seen as vital for a meaningful agreement which would come under the umbrella of the World Trade Organisation (WTO) and its book of rules.

The official said Washington had been encouraged by completion at the WTO over the past two months of global accords on liberalising telecommunications and removing tariffs from most information technology products.
"We feel this should provide momentum for the financial services talks," the official added.

Financial services cover banking, securities business, insurance, asset management and linked activities -- areas the WTO says account for $1.2 trillion a day in foreign exchange transactions around the globe.

A pact built on the 1995 interim deal, which was shaped by the European Union after the United States pulled out, would commit signatories to a phased removal of restrictions on foreign companies operating in their domestic markets.

The United States declined to join that accord -- which runs out at the end of this year -- because, it said, key developing countries were not ready to open up their financial service sector fast enough.

Their offers, it argued, were insufficient to justify throwing open the U.S. market, as would be required under the WTO's most-favoured-nation (MFN) rule which bars discriminatory treatment of selected trading partners.
In contrast, the EU said that although it would have liked more it felt offers then on the table were good enough to build on.

Some trade diplomats noted that the United States was proposing the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum (APEC) should issue a statement at a meeting in Canada next month in support of a financial services deal. This indicated that Washington was serious this time, they said.
Many of the Asian countries the United States is known to be pressing for better offers -- including Malaysia and Thailand -- are members of APEC.

But other WTO envoys in Geneva are less sure. "We do not yet see the sort of support from the U.S. financial services industry for a deal that we saw in telecommunications and information technology," said one.

The new talks will continue throughout the week with a meeting of a WTO negotiating group on Thursday to assess progress, although little concrete advance is expected until the autumn. The talks mark the third effort to get an agreement in the sector over the past five years.

The first was launched during the last two years of the 1986-93 Uruguay Round of world trade negotiations. But like a parallel effort to shape a telecommunications deal, it became bogged down and was set aside.

WTO officials say an accord would bring quick benefit to ordinary customers of banks, insurance companies and broking houses by giving them more service providers to chose from and -- because of competition -- a better deal.
